chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa from Ali ibn Ahmad from Musa ibn Umar from Muhammad ibn Mansur said:

I asked him about the one who forgets the second prostration of the second rak'ah, or is uncertain about it. He said: 'If you fear that you did not place your face [in prostration] except once, then when you have given the salam, prostrate with one prostration and place your face once, and there is no blame (sahw) upon you.'

So it is also not contradictory to what we mentioned, because his saying 'the one who forgets the final prostration of the second rak'ah' allows for the possibility that he meant the second rak'ah of the final two rak'ahs. And in the apparent text of the report, it is not [limited to] the second rak'ah of the first two, or the final two, but it is compatible with both together.
And when it is compatible with that, we apply it to the second rak'ah of the final two rak'ahs, and all the hadiths become consistent, by the grace and favor of Allah.

As for that which indicates the obligation of the two prostrations of forgetfulness (sajdat al-sahw) upon the one who left a prostration and did not mention it except after bowing, according to what he mentioned, may Allah have mercy on him.

key_terms.سَهْوٌ: Forgetfulness/blame (in the context of ritual error)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if I forget the second prostration in the second rak'ah of a four-rak'ah prayer?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* elucidates the specific mechanism of *sajdat al-tilawah* or *sajdat al-shakk* when a worshipper doubts the completion of the second prostration in the second rak'ah, ruling that a single post-salam prostration suffices without incurring the penalty of negligence. Al-Tusi’s commentary highlights the jurisprudential principle of interpreting ambiguous texts (*ikhtilaf*) in favor of the final two rak'ahs, ensuring harmony with other hadiths that mandate two prostrations of forgetfulness when a prostration is missed and recalled after bowing. This reflects the Shia emphasis on precision in ritual acts while providing leniency for genuine uncertainty.
